title: Meta's new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free
key_facts: Nieman Lab reported that Meta's new commercial terms appear to let it crawl and scrape websites associated with businesses that use its platforms, including publishers.
The terms take effect on 30 Oct 2026 and apply to business accounts promoting content on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger.
Meta may use the outside content to 'develop, improve, research' and 'train' its AI products.
Legal experts told Nieman Lab Meta could argue its commercial terms override blocking instructions such as a site's robots.txt file, and could bypass a licensing deal.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says Meta is only consolidating its commercial and self-serve ad terms and that there is no change to how it uses web crawlers; publishers can still use robots.txt flags.
Andy Stone, Meta's vice president of communications, says the change is meant to pull accurate product information from third-party shop sites, not to scrape news sites.
James Grimmelmann, professor of digital and information law at Cornell, told Nieman Lab it clearly gives Meta permission to train AI on any content from news publishers' sites.
Businesses that reject the terms 'may stop all access or use' of Meta's products for business purposes; Meta has also begun charging businesses to post links.
quote_evidence: While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like a site’s robots.txt file.
The new terms, which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products.
Update, October 16th: Added a statement from Meta and legal commentary.
why_it_matters_hint: Publishers could lose control over whether Meta trains its AI on their sites, while Meta says nothing has changed.
event_date: Nieman Lab report 15 Oct 2026; terms effective 30 Oct 2026
notes: Read at The Verge (updated 16 Oct with Meta's statement). Nieman Lab (first reporter, 15 Oct) was blocked by Cloudflare; its link was decoded from Google News and not opened.
